Q1402751.title: Battle of Pichincha
Q1402751.place: Slopes of the Pichincha volcano above Quito, Ecuador
paras: The war for the Presidency of Quito began when Guayaquil threw off Spanish rule in October 1820. Its first campaigns into the highlands were beaten back, and twice the patriots were defeated at Huachi, near Ambato, the second time in September 1821 under Antonio José de Sucre, whom Simón Bolívar had sent to help. In January 1822 Sucre opened a new campaign with about 1,700 men: recruits from Guayaquil and the highlands, Colombians, Spanish soldiers who had changed sides, and a battalion of British volunteers, the Albión. At Saraguro in February he was joined by a Peruvian division of about 1,500 men under Andrés de Santa Cruz, sent by José de San Martín. Cuenca fell without a shot in February, and the royalists withdrew north.

The Spanish commander, Field Marshal Melchor Aymerich, fortified the passes leading to Quito. Sucre went round them along the slopes of Cotopaxi into the Chillos valley, and the royalists fell back into the city. On the night of 23–24 May 1822 the patriot army, 2,971 men according to Wikipedia, climbed the Pichincha volcano above Quito to get past the defences. Rain turned the trails to mud; by dawn the troops were only halfway up, exhausted and in view of the royalist sentries, and Aymerich sent his army of 1,894 men up the mountain to meet them.

The two armies were thrown in piece by piece on steep slopes cut by gullies and thick undergrowth. Several patriot battalions, short of ammunition, fell back. In Wikipedia's account, Aymerich had sent his veteran Aragón battalion towards the summit to fall on the patriot rear, but it was stopped by the Albión, which arrived with the reserve ammunition on even higher ground; the Colombian Alto Magdalena battalion then charged and broke the royalist line. At midday Aymerich ordered a retreat. The fighting had lasted no more than three hours. Sucre's report counted 400 royalist and 200 patriot dead and 1,100 prisoners taken.

Sucre entered Quito on 25 May 1822, Wikipedia says, and accepted Aymerich's surrender. Quito was incorporated into the Republic of Colombia, which Bolívar entered in June, and Guayaquil was joined to Colombia in July. In 1830 Quito, Guayaquil and Cuenca broke away from Colombia to form the Republic of Ecuador. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates the battle to 22 May and puts the field at 10,200 feet; Wikipedia gives 24 May and 3,500 metres.

Q1441451.title: Guayaquil Conference
paras: By mid-1822 the two great liberation campaigns of South America had met. José de San Martín, Protector of Peru since 1821, held Lima, but a strong royalist army remained in the interior. Simón Bolívar had freed Venezuela and New Granada as the Republic of Colombia, and after Sucre's victory at Pichincha in May 1822, won with the help of a division San Martín had sent, Bolívar was master of Quito. The port of Guayaquil, independent since 1820, was divided between those who wanted to join Colombia, those who wanted to join Peru and those who wanted a state of their own. Bolívar entered the city with his troops in July and ended the argument by annexing it to Colombia.

San Martín arrived by sea on 25 July and landed the next day. Bolívar received him, and on 26 and 27 July the two men talked alone, for about an hour and a half on the first day and some four hours on the second, according to the Argentine historian Bartolomé Mitre; no account of what they said was published. At the banquet on 27 July Bolívar toasted 'the two greatest men of South America, General San Martín and myself', while San Martín drank to the speedy end of the war, the organization of the republics of the continent and the health of the Liberator of Colombia. San Martín left the ball in the early hours and sailed back to Peru.

What passed between them has been pieced together from later evidence. Both Wikipedia and Mitre say they differed over how to govern the liberated countries: San Martín favoured constitutional monarchies, Bolívar republics. San Martín wanted enough Colombian troops to finish the war in Peru and even offered to serve under Bolívar, who declined. Mitre adds that Bolívar offered only three battalions, saying he could not leave Colombian territory without the authority of his congress.

In Mitre's judgement San Martín now saw that one of the two had to give way. Back in Lima, where his minister Bernardo Monteagudo had been driven out in his absence, he laid down his authority before Peru's first congress on 20 September 1822 and left the country. Mitre quotes a letter to Bolívar in which San Martín wrote that his presence was the only obstacle keeping Bolívar and his army out of Peru. Bolívar took over the war there, which was decided at Ayacucho in December 1824.

cp08-19.title: Brazil declares independence
paras: When the French invaded Portugal in 1807, the Portuguese royal family fled to Brazil, and Rio de Janeiro became the seat of the monarchy; in 1815 Brazil was raised to a kingdom united with Portugal. The liberal revolution of 1820 in Portugal upset this arrangement. In February 1821 the Portuguese troops in Rio forced King John VI to accept the new constitutional system, and the king returned to Lisbon, leaving his heir, Pedro, as regent of Brazil. In Lisbon the Cortes began framing a constitution before Brazil's deputies arrived, and angry quarrels between Brazilian and Portuguese deputies followed.

When the Cortes ordered Pedro back to Europe, Brazilians feared that their country would fall back to colonial status; Wikipedia adds that the Cortes meant to reduce him to a mere military governor. The provisional government of São Paulo, led by the Andrada brothers, and then the council of Rio de Janeiro asked him to disobey and remain, and he agreed. The Portuguese troops in Rio were forced to embark for Portugal. Pedro took the Andradas into his ministry, accepted the title of Perpetual Defender of Brazil, and went to Minas Gerais and São Paulo to rally the provinces. On 7 September 1822, beside the Ipiranga brook at São Paulo, he declared Brazil independent of Portugal, the declaration remembered as the Cry of Ipiranga.

Back in Rio de Janeiro, Pedro was acclaimed constitutional emperor on 12 October 1822 and crowned that December. Portuguese forces still held Bahia, Piauí, Maranhão, Grão-Pará and the Cisplatine province, and a war followed. The Brazilians besieged Bahia until the Portuguese re-embarked on 2 July 1823, while a Brazilian squadron under Lord Cochrane attacked their ships, and by the end of 1823 the emperor's authority was accepted throughout the country.

Portugal recognized Brazil as an independent empire in a treaty of August 1825 (signed on the 25th, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica; Wikipedia gives 29 August). In return Brazil agreed to pay Portugal a large compensation, given by the Britannica as the Portuguese debt of nearly two million pounds sterling, and, Wikipedia adds, signed treaties with Britain to ban the Atlantic slave trade and give British goods preferential tariffs.

Q1508820.title: Battle of Junín
Q1508820.place: Plain of Junín, central highlands of Peru
paras: After San Martín left Peru in 1822 the patriot cause there went badly, and in February 1824 the royalists regained Lima. Simón Bolívar, who had come from Colombia to take charge, reorganized his army at Trujillo in the north and in June 1824 led it south into the highlands against the royalist army of Field Marshal José de Canterac. The two forces met on 6 August 1824 on the plain of Junín, a marshy plateau near Lake Junín at about 4,100 metres.

According to Wikipedia, Bolívar was hurrying to cut Canterac's retreat towards Cuzco and sent his cavalry, about 1,000 strong, ahead; Canterac sent some 1,300 horsemen to stop them while his infantry withdrew. The royalist charge struck the patriot cavalry while it was still forming up and drove much of it back in disorder; General Necochea was wounded and taken prisoner. One squadron of Peruvian hussars under Isidoro Suárez had not yet been engaged. It charged the scattered royalists in the flank and rear, the rest of the patriot cavalry under General Miller rallied, and the royalists broke and fled. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which calls Suárez a captain where Wikipedia has lieutenant colonel, likewise says the battle was won by a charge of the Peruvians under Suárez at the critical moment. Wikipedia adds that the charge was set off by an order that Major José Andrés Rázuri invented.

The fight was purely a cavalry action, with lance and sabre and no firearms, and lasted about 45 minutes; Wikipedia puts the dead at about 250 royalists and 150 patriots. The patriot infantry arrived only after it was over, and Bolívar renamed the Hussars of Peru the Hussars of Junín. Canterac's retreat went on, with many desertions. Bolívar returned to the coast, leaving Antonio José de Sucre to follow the royalists, and on 9 December 1824 Sucre's victory at Ayacucho ended Spanish rule in Peru.

Q2918225.title: Bolivian Declaration of Independence
paras: Upper Peru, the future Bolivia, saw almost continuous war from 1809: armies from Buenos Aires invaded it and were driven back, while patriot guerrillas held out in the mountains. In 1824 the royalist camp split when General Pedro Antonio Olañeta, an absolutist, rebelled against the liberal-minded viceroy La Serna. After the patriot victory at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824, Antonio José de Sucre marched into Upper Peru with part of his army.

News of Ayacucho set off a general rising, and royalist garrisons went over to the patriots one after another. Patriots under José Miguel Lanza took La Paz before Sucre arrived; Sucre crossed the Desaguadero River and entered La Paz in February. Olañeta, left with about 2,000 men according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, held out around Potosí until he was fatally wounded fighting some of his own troops who had turned against him: in March 1825, says the Britannica, and at Tumusla in early April, says Wikipedia, which adds that some sources deny there was a battle and say he shot himself. The last royalist force surrendered in April, according to Wikipedia.

In February 1825 Sucre summoned the provinces to send deputies to an assembly that would decide their future: union with the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, union with Peru, or full independence. Bolívar reproached Sucre privately for the initiative, but in May the congress at Buenos Aires declared that the provinces were at full liberty to decide their fate. The assembly met at Chuquisaca in July (on the 9th according to Wikipedia's article on the declaration, the 8th according to its article on Sucre) and voted for complete independence as a republic. The Act of Independence, drafted by a commission under the assembly's president, José Mariano Serrano, bears the date 6 August 1825, the first anniversary of Bolívar's victory at Junín. The 1911 Britannica puts the deputies at 54; Wikipedia's count of the signatories by province (7 from Charcas, 14 from Potosí, 12 from La Paz, 13 from Cochabamba and 2 from Santa Cruz) gives 48.

The assembly named the new state the Republic of Bolívar, soon changed to Bolivia, and declared the Liberator Father of the Republic. Bolívar, who had doubted that the country could stand on its own, declined the presidency in favour of Sucre. The assembly dissolved itself in October 1825; Bolívar signed a decree in Lima on 18 May 1826 by which Peru recognized Bolivia's independence, and a new congress adopted the constitution he had drafted, with Sucre as president. 6 August is Bolivia's Independence Day.

Q288251.title: Cisplatine War
Q288251.place: Banda Oriental (Uruguay) and the Río de la Plata
paras: In 1816 Portuguese forces from Brazil invaded the Banda Oriental, the land east of the Uruguay River, defeated José Gervasio Artigas and annexed it as the province of Cisplatina, which stayed with Brazil after Brazil's independence in 1822. The United Provinces of the Río de la Plata wanted it back, and a mission to Brazil in 1823 failed. In April 1825 the 'Thirty-Three Orientals' under Juan Antonio Lavalleja crossed from Buenos Aires and began a rising, and on 25 August a congress at Florida declared the province independent of Brazil and united with the United Provinces. After rebel victories at Rincón and Sarandí, the Argentine congress declared the province reincorporated in October, and in December 1825 Brazil declared war on the United Provinces.

Brazil blockaded the River Plate. On land, the Argentine army and the Oriental insurgents held the Uruguayan countryside but never took Montevideo or Colonia or got far into Brazil, while Brazil could neither win back the countryside nor gain a decisive victory. The largest battle was fought at Ituzaingó; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica counts it as a Brazilian defeat, while Wikipedia describes the war on land as a stalemate. At sea the Brazilian navy had the better of it and destroyed most of the small Argentine fleet of the Irish-born admiral William Brown, although the Argentines beat a Brazilian flotilla on the Uruguay River at Juncal. The blockade weighed heavily on Buenos Aires, and Brazil's seizures of foreign merchant ships led to disputes with the United States, France and Britain that Brazil later settled by paying compensation.

The cost of the war strained both countries. In 1827 the Argentine envoy Manuel José García, exceeding his instructions, signed a treaty giving up the province; President Bernardino Rivadavia rejected it, but the outcry helped bring about his resignation, and Manuel Dorrego, as governor of Buenos Aires, carried on the war. Under British mediation, and pressure on the emperor according to the Britannica, the two sides signed a Preliminary Peace Convention on 27 August 1828, by which the province became an independent state, the future Eastern Republic of Uruguay, formally constituted in 1830. (The Britannica's article on Argentina dates Uruguay's independence to 1827; its articles on Brazil and Uruguay give 1828.) In Buenos Aires the peace was followed by civil war: the Unitarian general Juan Lavalle overthrew Dorrego and had him shot in December 1828.

cp10-02.title: Frankfurt Parliament opens
cp10-02.place: St Paul's Church (Paulskirche), Frankfurt am Main
paras: The revolutions of March 1848 shook every government in the German Confederation. Liberal deputies from several state assemblies, meeting at Heidelberg, invited present and former members of the German diets to Frankfurt, and on 30 March the federal diet itself, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, authorized a national parliament. The resulting Pre-Parliament met in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt at the end of March. Its moderate liberal majority chose to work with the federal diet, left a Committee of Fifty to represent it until a national assembly met, and fixed one deputy for every 50,000 inhabitants. Some radicals who wanted more left it, and a republican rising they called in Baden was put down.

The elections were held under each state's own rules. They were limited to 'independent' adult men, which Wikipedia estimates still let about 85% of men vote, and Czech-majority districts in Bohemia and Moravia boycotted them. The National Assembly opened in St Paul's Church on 18 May 1848, the first freely elected parliament for all the German states, including the German-speaking lands of the Austrian Empire, and the next day it chose Heinrich von Gagern as its president. Late in June it created a Provisional Central Power and elected Archduke John of Austria as imperial regent (Reichsverweser); in July the old federal diet handed its responsibilities over to him.

The assembly then set out to write a constitution, and its debates dragged on through the crises of 1848: the war over Schleswig-Holstein, the question of whether Austria belonged in the new Germany, and the recovery of the princes' power. The Britannica blames 'learned professors and talkative journalists' and their endless speeches for the lost time. In 1849 the assembly adopted a constitution for a German Empire with a hereditary emperor and offered the crown to King Frederick William IV of Prussia, who refused it; the Britannica quotes him as refusing 'to pick up a crown out of the gutter'. Austria and Prussia recalled their deputies, most of the rest resigned on 21 May 1849, and a radical rump that moved to Stuttgart was dispersed on 18 June 1849 by order of the Württemberg government.

Q837787.title: Battle of Novara
paras: In 1848 King Charles Albert of Sardinia-Piedmont had gone to war with Austria in support of the risings in Lombardy and Venetia, but after his defeat at Custoza he accepted an armistice. By early 1849 the revolutionary movement elsewhere in Italy was breaking down, yet the king felt he could not abandon the Lombards and Venetians, and on 12 March 1849 he denounced the armistice. Lacking confidence in his own generals after 1848, he gave the chief command to the Polish general Chrzanowski. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts his forces at 80,000 men, including Lombard and other volunteers, and says their discipline and morale had been shaken.

The Austrian commander, Field Marshal Joseph Radetzky, took the initiative at once. General Girolamo Ramorino, commanding the Lombard division, failed, against his instructions according to the Britannica, to stop the Austrians from crossing the Ticino and seizing the fortress town of Mortara, and the armies met at Novara, about 45 km west of Milan. The Austrians thoroughly routed the Piedmontese; Wikipedia cites estimates of 41,000 to 70,000 Austrians and 45,000 to 59,000 Piedmontese. The Britannica dates the battle to 23 March 1849 and says the king sought death in vain all day; Wikipedia says the fighting lasted through 22 March and ended at dawn on the 23rd. Ramorino was later court-martialled and shot.

Radetzky's terms included the occupation of part of Piedmont and the heir to the throne as a hostage. Thinking that his son might obtain better terms, Charles Albert abdicated in favour of Victor Emmanuel II and left at once for Portugal; he died in a monastery at Oporto on 28 July 1849. Victor Emmanuel met Radetzky on 24 March. According to the Britannica, the marshal offered to waive his territorial demands if the new king abolished the constitution, and Victor Emmanuel refused, accepting a temporary Austrian occupation of territory between the Po, the Ticino and the Sesia instead. Peace was signed on 9 August 1849, with an indemnity of 65 million francs, Wikipedia says. Novara left Austria free to restore the old rulers elsewhere in Italy, but Piedmont kept its constitution.

Q2914928.title: Australian gold rushes
Q2914928.place: New South Wales and Victoria, Australia
paras: Gold had been found in New South Wales several times before 1851, but the colonial government kept the news quiet for fear of losing its workforce and unsettling the economy. When the California gold rush began in 1848 and drew people away from Australia, the government sought the Colonial Office's approval to exploit minerals and offered rewards for finding gold. Edward Hargraves, who had worked the Californian goldfields and learned panning and cradling there, found specks of alluvial gold with John Lister at Ophir, near Orange, in February 1851. After he claimed the discovery of payable gold, Australia's first gold rush began there in May 1851.

Victoria became a separate colony in 1851, and gold was found there a few weeks later. A rush to Clunes began in July 1851, and the fields of Ballarat and Bendigo followed from September. Who found gold first at each field was long disputed, and claimants such as the journalist Henry Frencham were later examined by a parliamentary select committee. Diggers came first from the neighbouring colonies, some of which, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says, were almost emptied of able-bodied men and women, and then from Europe and America. Victoria's population, 77,435 at separation according to the Britannica, was 236,778 at the 1854 census.

The miners resented the licence fee charged for the right to dig and their lack of any representation in the colony's legislature. At Ballarat in December 1854 the discontent ended in fighting with troops, with considerable loss of life on both sides; the licence fee was later replaced by an export duty on gold and a miner's right that also gave a small plot to live on. Over the longer run the rushes turned convict colonies into societies of free immigrants: Australia's total population rose nearly fourfold, from 430,000 in 1851 to 1.7 million in 1871, and by the end of 1905 Victoria's gold had been worth over £273 million, according to the Britannica.

cp09-03.title: Confederate States of America formed
paras: Abraham Lincoln's election as president in 1860 led seven slave states of the Deep South (South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas) to declare their secession from the United States over the winter of 1860–1861. Their principal aim, Wikipedia says, was to safeguard slavery: they feared northern abolitionist influence and federal interference with slave property, and expected that Lincoln's refusal to let slavery spread into the western territories would bring in more free states and eventually end it.

Southern leaders met at Montgomery, Alabama, in February 1861, and on 8 February, Wikipedia says, the seven states formed the Confederate States of America under a provisional constitution describing a confederation of 'sovereign and independent states'. Jefferson Davis of Mississippi, a former army officer, congressman and federal cabinet member, was chosen provisional president, and Alexander H. Stephens became vice-president. A permanent constitution followed in March 1861. Much of it copied the United States Constitution, but it stressed the rights of the states, explicitly protected slavery, let the president veto single items in appropriation bills, forbade bounties or taxes for the benefit of particular industries, and limited the president to one term: six years according to Wikipedia, seven according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.

The war began in April 1861, when Confederate forces attacked and took Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour. After Lincoln called up 75,000 militia, four states of the Upper South (Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina) seceded and joined the Confederacy. No foreign government recognized it. Over four years of war its government at Richmond grew more centralized, provoking bitter states'-rights opposition, Stephens among the critics. The Confederacy collapsed in 1865: Robert E. Lee surrendered on 9 April, and most Confederate forces had ceased fighting by May.

cp10-06.title: Kingdom of Italy proclaimed
paras: In 1859 the Kingdom of Sardinia (Piedmont), allied with France, fought Austria in the Second Italian War of Independence and won Lombardy; under the secret Plombières agreement it ceded Savoy and Nice to France. In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand overthrew Bourbon rule in Sicily and Naples, while Piedmontese troops occupied central Italy and part of the Papal States, though not Rome.

Garibaldi met King Victor Emmanuel II in late October 1860 (on the 26th, at Teano, according to Wikipedia; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the 29th) and hailed him as King of Italy, setting aside republican hopes for the sake of unity under the monarchy. The two entered Naples together on 7 November; Garibaldi then handed his authority to the king, refused the title and honours offered to him, and retired to his island of Caprera. The last Bourbon strongholds fell early in 1861: Gaeta surrendered on 13 February and Civitella del Tronto on 21 March.

The first Italian parliament met at Turin on 18 February 1861, and Victor Emmanuel, King of Sardinia since March 1849, became King of Italy, 'by the grace of God and by the will of the nation', under the law of 17 March 1861. (The Britannica's account places his proclamation at the parliament's opening.) The title had not been used since Napoleon gave it up in 1814. Britain recognized the new kingdom within a fortnight and France three months later. It covered the whole peninsula except Venetia and Rome, which, the Britannica says, the government and nation were determined to annex sooner or later. Venetia followed after the war of 1866 and Rome in 1870.

Q868481.title: Battle of Hampton Roads
paras: When Union forces abandoned the Gosport navy yard near Norfolk, Virginia, in the spring of 1861, they set fire to the warships there. The Confederates raised one of them, the steam frigate Merrimack, and rebuilt her as an ironclad ram renamed CSS Virginia: cut down to the waterline and topped with a sloping casemate of heavy timber covered with iron, armed with ten guns and an iron ram, but slow and hard to turn. The aim was to break the Union blockade that had cut Norfolk and Richmond off from overseas trade. The Union's answer was John Ericsson's USS Monitor, a low-lying ironclad carrying two heavy guns in a revolving turret, launched on 30 January 1862; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records that she was mocked as a 'Yankee cheese-box on a raft'.

On 8 March 1862 the Virginia, commanded by Franklin Buchanan, steamed down the Elizabeth River with supporting gunboats to attack the wooden Union ships in Hampton Roads. She rammed and sank the sloop Cumberland, and the frigate Congress, which had run aground, was forced to surrender and was set on fire. Buchanan was wounded, and Lieutenant Catesby ap Roger Jones took command. The steam frigate Minnesota had also run aground, in water too shallow for the Virginia to reach her, so as evening came the Confederates drew off, meaning to finish her the next day.

That night the Monitor, under Lieutenant John L. Worden, arrived from New York after a dangerous voyage and took up position beside the Minnesota. On the morning of 9 March she came out to meet the Virginia, and the first fight between ironclad warships lasted some three hours. Neither ship could seriously damage the other; according to the Britannica, not one shot pierced either's armour. After a shot struck the Monitor's pilot house and blinded Worden, the Monitor drew off, and the Virginia returned to Norfolk. The battle was indecisive, but the blockade stayed in place.

The two ships never met again. When the Confederates evacuated Norfolk in May 1862 they scuttled the Virginia, which could not be taken up the James River, and the Monitor sank in a gale off Cape Hatteras on 31 December 1862. The battle drew attention around the world. Britain and France stopped building wooden-hulled warships, turreted 'monitors' were built on the Monitor's model, and the Britannica calls the battle the opening of the era of the armoured warship.

Q1066253.title: Siege of Vicksburg
paras: Vicksburg, a fortress city on high bluffs above the Mississippi, was the last major Confederate stronghold on the river. In the spring of 1863 the Union general Ulysses S. Grant, with the Army of the Tennessee, set out to take it from the Confederate army of Lieutenant-General John C. Pemberton. Attempts to reach the high ground north of the city through the swamps and waterways had failed.

Grant then marched his troops overland, through a network of lakes and streams, to a point south of Vicksburg, while on 16 April Admiral David Porter's gunboats and the transports ran past the city's batteries. At the end of April the army crossed to the east bank below Grand Gulf, drove off the Confederates at Port Gibson and, in early May, cut loose from its base of supplies. Grant struck east, fought at Raymond on 12 May and took Jackson, keeping Pemberton apart from the relief force of General Joseph E. Johnston. On 16 May he defeated Pemberton at Champion Hill and drove him back into Vicksburg's lines.

By 19 May the city was invested by land and water. Assaults on 19 and 22 May were thrown back with heavy losses, and Grant settled into a siege, digging approaches and mines towards the Confederate works while Johnston's force was held off to the east. Under heavy bombardment from the gunboats and the army's artillery, the townspeople sheltered in caves dug into the clay hills.

With supplies nearly gone, Pemberton opened talks. Grant at first demanded unconditional surrender, then agreed to parole the prisoners rather than ship them north, and the garrison surrendered on 4 July 1863, the day after the Union victory at Gettysburg. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica's articles on Vicksburg and on the war put the surrendered garrison at 37,000, its article on Grant at 29,491; Wikipedia gives 29,495 surrendered out of 32,697 Confederate casualties, against 4,835 Union casualties for the battle and siege.

Port Hudson, downriver, surrendered to General Nathaniel Banks a few days later, giving the Union control of the whole Mississippi and cutting off Arkansas, Texas and part of Louisiana from the rest of the Confederacy. Lincoln, as Wikipedia quotes him, said that 'the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea'. The Britannica calls the capture perhaps the greatest Union success of the war.

Q756118.title: Atlanta campaign
paras: In the spring of 1864 Ulysses S. Grant, now general-in-chief of the Union armies, left William T. Sherman in command in the west. Sherman gathered three armies near Chattanooga, the Army of the Tennessee under McPherson, the Army of the Cumberland under Thomas and the Army of the Ohio under Schofield, and in early May invaded Georgia, aiming at Atlanta. Facing him was the Confederate Army of Tennessee under General Joseph E. Johnston, which was much smaller: Wikipedia gives 98,500 Union troops on paper against 50,000, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts Sherman's three armies at 100,000 men.

For two months the campaign was one of manoeuvre. Each time Sherman worked round a flank, at Rocky Face Ridge, Resaca and Adairsville, Johnston fell back to a prepared line, and heavy fighting followed around Dallas and New Hope Church in late May. Near Marietta Sherman tried frontal attacks instead, and his assault on Kennesaw Mountain on 27 June was thrown back. He returned to flanking moves, turned Johnston's line on the Chattahoochee in early July, and Johnston withdrew into the Atlanta defences.

Jefferson Davis, impatient with the retreats, replaced Johnston in mid-July with General John B. Hood, who was expected to fight. Hood attacked at once, at Peachtree Creek on 20 July and in the Battle of Atlanta a few days later, in which the Union general McPherson was killed, and again at Ezra Church on 28 July; each attack was beaten off. With the city nearly surrounded, the fighting around Jonesboro to the south settled the campaign.

Hood evacuated Atlanta, and Union troops entered it: the Britannica says Sherman took the city on 1 September; Wikipedia says Hood left on the night of 1 September, destroying the ammunition trains, and General Henry Slocum's troops occupied the city on 2 September. Losses were heavy on both sides; Wikipedia gives 31,687 Union and 34,979 Confederate casualties, and the Britannica a Union loss of 30,000.

Hood's army escaped, which Wikipedia notes left the campaign's first aim unmet, but the fall of Atlanta lifted Northern morale and, according to Wikipedia, helped to re-elect President Abraham Lincoln. Sherman ordered the remaining civilians out of the city and, in November, set out from Atlanta on his March to the Sea.

Q1052780.title: Sherman's March to the Sea
paras: After taking Atlanta in September 1864, the Union general William T. Sherman faced the Confederate Army of Tennessee under John B. Hood, which moved north to strike at his supply line and then into Tennessee. Sherman sent George H. Thomas back to defend Tennessee and resolved instead to march through Georgia to the sea, destroying everything of military value on the way. Lincoln and Grant had doubts, but Grant approved the plan in early November.

Sherman cut his railway link with the north, wrecked Atlanta as a military base and set out on 15 November with picked troops: 62,000 men according to Wikipedia, 60,000 or 50,000 in two articles of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The army moved in two wings, under Oliver O. Howard and Henry Slocum, with Judson Kilpatrick's cavalry, and lived off the country by organized foraging. Little stood in its way: Hood had taken most Confederate forces to Tennessee, leaving William J. Hardee with militia and Joseph Wheeler's cavalry.

The columns feinted towards Macon and Augusta, beat off a Georgia militia attack at Griswoldville and took the state capital, Milledgeville, while tearing up railways and stripping a belt of country some 60 miles wide, in the Britannica's figure. On 10 December the army reached the defences of Savannah, and on 13 December a division stormed Fort McAllister, opening contact with the Union fleet.

Hardee chose not to surrender and slipped his troops out across the Savannah River on 20 December. The Britannica dates the occupation of Savannah to that day; Wikipedia says the mayor surrendered the city the next morning, 21 December. Sherman then telegraphed Lincoln, as Wikipedia quotes him, offering the city 'as a Christmas gift'.

The march cut the Confederacy's railways and supplies and, the Britannica says, severed its government from the western states. Wikipedia notes that some historians see Sherman's 'hard war' against property as an early form of total war. In January 1865 Sherman turned north through the Carolinas.

Q1355391.title: Battle of Appomattox Court House and Lee's surrender
paras: From June 1864 General Robert E. Lee's Confederate Army of Northern Virginia held the trenches around Petersburg and Richmond against the Union armies of Ulysses S. Grant. At the start of April 1865 Philip Sheridan's victory at Five Forks turned Lee's flank and the Union infantry broke through the Petersburg lines. Lee abandoned Petersburg and Richmond and retreated west, hoping to join General Joseph E. Johnston's army in North Carolina.

The retreat went badly. Lee's starving men found no rations waiting at Amelia Court House, and at Sailor's Creek a large part of the army, including Richard Ewell's corps, was cut off and captured. Grant wrote to Lee suggesting surrender, and Lee asked what terms he had in mind. Sheridan's cavalry got ahead of the Confederates at Appomattox Station, seized the supply trains waiting there and blocked the road west, while Union infantry hurried up behind.

At dawn on 9 April John B. Gordon's corps attacked Sheridan's cavalry and pushed it back, but from the ridge his men saw two Union infantry corps drawn up in front of them. With his way out closed, Lee asked for a truce and rode to meet Grant. That afternoon, in the parlour of Wilmer McLean's house in the village of Appomattox Court House, he surrendered his army.

Under the terms the Confederates gave up their arms and military stores and signed paroles not to fight again; Wikipedia adds that they could keep their horses and officers their sidearms. At a formal ceremony three days later (12 April, according to Wikipedia) the army stacked its arms and was disbanded, and Wikipedia gives nearly 28,000 officers and men paroled. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the victors made no show of triumph and made the lot of the vanquished as easy as possible.

Lee's surrender did not formally end the war, but other commanders followed: Johnston surrendered to William T. Sherman near Durham, North Carolina, on 26 April, and the remaining Confederate forces soon after. For the Britannica, the Confederacy came to an end at Appomattox; the formal end of the war came with the president's general amnesty of 29 May 1865.

cp10-07.title: Bismarck becomes Minister President of Prussia
paras: King William I of Prussia, who had governed for his ailing brother since 1857 and reigned as king since 1861, wanted to enlarge and reorganize the army, a reform carried through with his war minister Albrecht von Roon. The Liberal majority in the Prussian parliament refused to vote the money. In March 1862 the king dissolved the chamber, but the elections returned an even larger Liberal majority, and in September the lower house threw out the budget by a large majority. The king even thought of abdicating.

Otto von Bismarck, a Junker and former ultra-conservative deputy, had been Prussia's delegate to the German diet at Frankfurt and then ambassador in St Petersburg. The king had hesitated to appoint him because Bismarck wanted a free hand in foreign affairs, and in 1862 sent him as ambassador to Paris instead (in May, according to Wikipedia; in June, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica). In September 1862, on Roon's advice, the king summoned Bismarck to Berlin and made him minister-president and foreign minister; Wikipedia dates the appointment to 23 September.

A week later, on 30 September, Bismarck told the budget committee of the chamber that the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes but by 'blood and iron'. His appointment caused intense indignation and his early fall was widely predicted. Instead he governed without an approved budget for four years, arguing that the constitution did not say what should happen when the king and parliament failed to agree and collecting taxes on the basis of the last budget.

The reorganized army won the wars against Denmark, which lost Schleswig and Holstein in 1864, and against Austria in 1866, after which the chamber passed a bill of indemnity for the government's breaches of the constitution. Bismarck remained minister-president of Prussia, with one short break, until 1890, and became the first chancellor of the German Empire in 1871.

cp10-11.title: North German Confederation formed
paras: Prussia's victory over Austria in the war of 1866 ended the old German Confederation. In the peace signed at Prague on 23 August 1866 Austria accepted a new organization of Germany without itself, with a closer union to be founded by the king of Prussia north of the river Main, while the states south of the Main were left to form their own union. Prussia annexed outright Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau and the free city of Frankfurt, as well as Schleswig and Holstein.

Prussia and the other north German states had already agreed, in August 1866, on an alliance that was to become a federal state under a constitution. A constituent parliament, elected by universal manhood suffrage, met in Berlin on 24 February 1867 and accepted, with some changes, a draft drawn up on the lines laid down by Prussia's minister-president, Otto von Bismarck. Wikipedia gives the final vote, on 16 April 1867, as 230 to 53, and dates the constitution's coming into force to 1 July 1867, with Bismarck appointed federal chancellor soon afterwards.

The king of Prussia held the presidency of the confederation by hereditary right and commanded its army and navy. Laws needed the approval of a federal council (Bundesrat) of the states' governments and of a Reichstag elected by all adult men. Prussia had about four-fifths of the territory and people; according to Wikipedia it held 17 of the 43 votes in the Bundesrat but could easily build a majority with the small states.

The new parliament worked to unify the north legally and administratively, with laws on free movement, a common postal system, weights and measures and a penal code. A treaty of 1867 with Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse-Darmstadt joined them in a customs parliament, but the southern elections of 1868 returned many opponents of union with Prussia. The southern states joined only after fighting beside the confederation against France in 1870, and the enlarged federation became the German Empire in 1871.

Q2604547.title: Capture of Rome
paras: After 1861 the new Kingdom of Italy still lacked Rome, which Pope Pius IX ruled as the last remnant of the Papal States under the protection of a French garrison. In July 1870 France went to war with Prussia and withdrew its troops. On 18 July the Vatican Council, sitting in Rome, proclaimed papal infallibility. When Napoleon III fell after his defeat at Sedan in early September, the agreement by which Italy had promised France to respect papal Rome lost its force.

King Victor Emmanuel II wrote to the pope offering Italian protection in place of his temporal power, with guarantees for his independence, carried by Count Gustavo Ponza di San Martino. Pius refused and said he would yield only to force. On 11 September General Raffaele Cadorna led Italian troops into papal territory, and Civitavecchia surrendered. The sources give the forces differently: about 50,000 Italians against 13,157 papal troops in Wikipedia, 60,000 against 10,000 in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The papal army under General Hermann Kanzler included the Swiss Guard and the volunteer Papal Zouaves from many countries.

The pope decided on enough resistance to show that he was yielding to force. Early on 20 September 1870 the Italian artillery opened fire on the Aurelian Walls, and after a few hours a breach was made near the Porta Pia. The pope ordered his troops to cease fire, Italian soldiers poured into the city, and Kanzler signed a capitulation. Wikipedia gives 49 Italian and 19 papal soldiers killed. The Leonine City around the Vatican was left out of the capitulation; according to the Britannica, Italian troops occupied it the next day at the pope's request.

A plebiscite held in Rome on 2 October gave 133,681 votes for union with Italy and 1,507 against. A royal decree then joined Rome and Lazio to the kingdom. Pius denounced the vote and excommunicated the invaders, the king among them. Rome became the capital of Italy, officially in February 1871 according to Wikipedia; the Britannica dates the declaration to the king's solemn entry in July 1872. The capture ended the Papal States and the popes' temporal rule, and completed the unification of Italy.

Q4497452.title: Russian conquest of Khiva (1873)
Q4497452.place: Khanate of Khiva (Khorezm), on the lower Amu Darya
paras: Russia had twice failed to subdue the Khanate of Khiva, an oasis state on the lower Oxus (Amu Darya) surrounded by desert: in 1717 the force of Prince Bekovich-Cherkassky was destroyed, and in 1839 Count Perovsky's march from Orenburg was turned back by a cold winter. By 1868 Russia had taken Tashkent and Samarkand and controlled Kokand and Bukhara, and in 1869 it founded Krasnovodsk on the eastern shore of the Caspian. In 1871 and 1872, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says, the desert routes to Khiva were explored and surveyed.

In 1873 a carefully organized expedition under the governor-general of Turkestan, General Konstantin von Kaufmann, set out from several bases at once: from Tashkent and Fort Aralsk in the east, from Orenburg in the north, and from the Caspian shore in the west. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica puts the army at 10,000 men, and Wikipedia's article on the khanate at 13,000. The marches in spring through waterless desert cost many camels; the column from the south-eastern Caspian shore ran out of water and had to turn back.

Kaufmann reached the Oxus in late May and crossed it, while the Orenburg and Caspian columns joined in the north of the oasis and advanced on the capital. The khan fled and Khiva was occupied with little resistance: Wikipedia dates the city's fall to 10 June 1873, after a bombardment by the northern column, when Kaufmann entered peacefully.

Under the peace treaty of August 1873 (on the 12th, according to one Wikipedia article, the 24th according to another) the khan, restored to his throne, became a Russian protectorate: he gave up independent foreign relations, abolished slavery and the slave trade, and agreed to pay a heavy war indemnity. The Britannica says that all the khanate's land on the right bank of the Oxus was annexed to Russia, and that many thousands of slaves, mostly Persians, were set free. Khiva remained under Russian protection until the revolution of 1917.

cp18-102.title: Russian Turkestan created
paras: Russia had been pushing into the Central Asian steppe for decades, taking forts of the Khanate of Kokand in the 1850s. In 1864 columns from Siberia and Orenburg advanced to close the gap between their lines, and in 1865 General Mikhail Chernyayev took the city of Tashkent, going beyond his orders; the government in St Petersburg accepted the conquest. Khujand (Hodjent) and other towns followed, after a Russian victory over the Emir of Bukhara.

The new territory was at first a province under the governor-general of Orenburg. A special commission sent to study the country, known as the Steppe Commission, travelled through it for two years and in the spring of 1867 produced a plan for its government. A committee of the ministries of war, the interior and foreign affairs, chaired by the minister of war, accepted it with changes: Turkestan was detached from Orenburg, joined with Semirechye, taken from the Siberian province of Semipalatinsk, and put under a governor-general of its own, reporting directly to the emperor. The governor-general of Orenburg protested in vain.

The governor-general, appointed by the emperor, also commanded the troops and had full power to conduct relations with the neighbouring states. The first holder was General Konstantin von Kaufmann, who arrived in Tashkent, the capital, in late 1867. The province at first had two regions, Syr Darya and Semirechye. The traveller Eugene Schuyler, in his book Turkistan, judged that experience had proved the Orenburg governor-general's objections sound.

Turkestan grew as the conquest went on: the Zeravshan district around Samarkand, taken from Bukhara in 1868, the land on the right bank of the Amu Darya taken from Khiva in 1873, and the Fergana region formed from the Khanate of Kokand in 1876. Bukhara and Khiva survived as Russian protectorates, with internal autonomy but under Russian control of their foreign affairs. The governor-generalship lasted until the Russian Revolution.

cp18-104.title: Russia annexes Kokand
paras: By 1875 the Khanate of Kokand, in the Fergana Valley, had lost Tashkent and its northern lands to Russia, and its ruler Khudayar Khan was dependent on the Russians, with whom he had made a commercial treaty in 1868. Khudayar was unpopular at home: Wikipedia and the traveller Eugene Schuyler both point to his oppressive rule and taxes. In 1875 a revolt against him and against Russian influence spread through the khanate; his eldest son Nasreddin and much of his army went over to the rebels, led by Abdurrahman Aftobatcha. Khudayar fled with Russian envoys to Hodjent (Khujand) in Russian territory.

The rebels raised a holy war against Russia, and the governor-general of Turkestan, Konstantin von Kaufmann, invaded. He stormed the frontier fortress of Makhram and occupied the city of Kokand. The new khan, Nasreddin, made peace: according to Schuyler he agreed to pay an indemnity of 3,000,000 rubles over six years and ceded the part of the khanate north of the Syr Darya, around Namangan (the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says the land north of the Naryn).

The peace did not hold. The people of Kokand drove out Nasreddin, a pretender calling himself Pulat Bek was proclaimed khan, and fighting went on through the winter, with heavy destruction at Andijan and in the countryside, led on the Russian side by Mikhail Skobelev. In early 1876 Andijan was taken, Abdurrahman surrendered and Skobelev occupied Kokand.

In February 1876 (the Britannica's date) the khanate came to an end: the emperor ordered its annexation, and it became the Russian province of Fergana, the land's ancient name, under Skobelev as its first governor, according to Schuyler. Nasreddin and other leaders were sent as prisoners to Tashkent, and Pulat Bek was later captured and hanged.

Q10354157.title: Proclamation of the German Empire
Q10354157.place: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles
paras: After Prussia's victory over Austria in 1866, Otto von Bismarck united the German states north of the Main in the North German Confederation under the king of Prussia, while Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse-Darmstadt stayed outside. In July 1870 France declared war on Prussia, and the southern states, bound by defensive alliances, fought on Prussia's side. The German victories of August and September 1870 made the southern princes willing to join a united Germany.

In November 1870 the southern states signed treaties joining the confederation. In December the federal council and the Reichstag voted to rename it the German Empire (Deutsches Reich) and to give the king of Prussia the title of German Emperor, and the new constitution took effect on 1 January 1871. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the proclamation came on the initiative of the king of Bavaria, the most powerful of the southern rulers.

On 18 January 1871, while German armies were besieging Paris, King William I of Prussia was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors of the Palace of Versailles, the seat of the German headquarters. Wikipedia describes the ceremony: delegations of the regiments filled the hall with their banners, a religious service was held, Bismarck read out the proclamation, and the Grand Duke of Baden called for cheers for 'Emperor William', avoiding the exact title 'German Emperor', to which William objected. Wikipedia adds that the day was chosen as the anniversary of the coronation of the first king in Prussia in 1701.

Paris capitulated ten days later. In the Treaty of Frankfurt of 10 May 1871 France ceded Alsace and most of Lorraine to the new empire. Bismarck became its first chancellor, and the states of the North German Confederation formed the core of the German Empire.

Q808027.title: Treaty of Bardo: French protectorate over Tunisia
Q808027.place: Ksar Saïd palace, Le Bardo, near Tunis
paras: Tunisia, ruled by its own beys under nominal Ottoman suzerainty, went bankrupt, according to the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, in 1869 and its finances were put under British, French and Italian controllers. At the Congress of Berlin, in the Britannica's account, the British foreign secretary, Lord Salisbury, agreed to give France a free hand in Tunisia in return for French acceptance of Britain's lease of Cyprus. France held back until Italian activity in Tunisia, such as the purchase of the British-owned railway from Tunis to Goletta (La Goulette) in 1880, pushed it to act.

In April 1881 a French force crossed the frontier from Algeria, with raids by the Khroumir (Kroumir) tribes into Algeria as the pretext. Wikipedia puts the expedition at about 36,000 men. Meeting little resistance, the French advanced on Tunis, and on 12 May 1881 the bey, Muhammad as-Sadiq, signed the treaty at his Ksar Saïd palace at Le Bardo.

The treaty made Tunisia a French protectorate. France took charge of its foreign relations and could occupy points in the country, presented as a temporary measure to restore order and protect the bey. The conquest was not completed without a serious struggle, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes, especially at Sfax. The Conventions of La Marsa of 8 June 1883 extended French control to internal affairs, under a French resident-general.

For Italy, which had taken a deep interest in Tunisia's future, the affair began a long period of tension with France. The Ottoman Empire, which still claimed Tunisia, refused to recognize the protectorate, but its protests were ignored. Britain gave up its consular courts in Tunisia in 1883, and the other powers followed, Italy, the Britannica says, only in 1896.

Q1420382.title: Battle of Tel el-Kebir
Q1420382.place: Tel el-Kebir, between Ismailia and Cairo, Egypt
paras: In September 1881, the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records, an army movement led by Ahmed Urabi (Arabi Pasha) forced the khedive Tawfiq to enlarge the army, change his prime minister and summon an assembly of notables. In 1882 Urabi became minister of war, and the new government clashed with the European controllers of Egypt's debts. British and French warships came to Alexandria, and in June riots there cost many European lives. When Urabi went on arming the harbour forts and France refused to take part, the British fleet bombarded Alexandria on 11 July 1882, and British troops landed and occupied the city.

Sir Garnet Wolseley was given command of an expedition to crush Urabi's government and restore the khedive's authority; Wikipedia gives 24,000 British troops and 7,000 from India. Urabi's lines at Kafr el-Dawwar blocked the direct road from Alexandria to Cairo, so Wolseley moved his army through the Suez Canal, which Urabi had not blocked, and occupied Ismailia in August. Advancing west along the railway and the Sweet Water Canal, his troops beat off Egyptian attacks at Kassassin.

Urabi's main army had dug in at Tel el-Kebir. Wolseley found that the Egyptians kept no outposts at night, and on the night of 12 September his infantry marched across the flat desert to make a frontal attack at dawn. On 13 September 1882, as day broke, they were close to the entrenchments before being seen, and stormed them with the bayonet; Wikipedia says the fighting was over within an hour. Official British figures gave 57 British dead; Wikipedia gives about two thousand Egyptian dead.

British cavalry rode on to Cairo, which was undefended, and Urabi surrendered there. He was tried for rebellion, pleaded guilty and was exiled to Ceylon, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records, until 1901. The khedive's power was restored, but under British occupation: most of the army went home from November, leaving an army of occupation behind. Wolseley was made a peer as Baron Wolseley of Cairo.

cp11-06.title: Fall of Khartoum
paras: In 1881 Muhammad Ahmad, a holy man on the White Nile, proclaimed himself the Mahdi and led a revolt against Egyptian rule in the Sudan. Egypt, itself torn by Urabi's revolt and then occupied by Britain, could not stop it, and an Egyptian expedition under Hicks Pasha ended in disaster. In December 1883 the British government told Egypt to abandon the Sudan, and it sent General Charles Gordon, a former governor-general of the Sudan, to report on and carry out the evacuation of the Egyptian garrisons, soldiers, officials and their families.

Gordon reached Khartoum on 18 February 1884 as the khedive's governor-general and began sending women, children and the sick downriver; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says about two thousand five hundred left before the Mahdi's forces closed in. His request that the influential Zubayr Pasha be made ruler of the Sudan was refused because Zubayr had been a slave-trader, and wavering tribes went over to the Mahdi. When Berber surrendered, Khartoum was cut off. The siege began in March 1884 (on the 13th, according to Wikipedia; on the 18th, according to the Britannica). Wikipedia gives about 7,000 Egyptian troops and 27,000 civilians in the city.

Only in August, under the pressure of public opinion, did the British government decide to send a relief force under Lord Wolseley up the Nile. A column crossed the Bayuda desert and, after hard fighting, reached the Nile near Metemma in January 1885, where steamers sent by Gordon were waiting. Meanwhile Khartoum was starving.

On the night of 25-26 January 1885 the Mahdists, able to wade across the Nile at its seasonal low, broke into the city. The weakened garrison was killed, and Wikipedia gives 4,000 male civilians killed and many women and children enslaved. Gordon died in the attack; accounts of his death differ, and his head was taken to the Mahdi at Omdurman. Sir Charles Wilson reached Khartoum by steamer on 28 January and found it fallen two days before.

The relief force was withdrawn, and the Sudan was left to the Mahdi, who founded a religious state but died in June 1885. Gordon was mourned in Britain as a martyr, and the Sudan was retaken only by Kitchener's army, which defeated the Mahdists at Omdurman in 1898.

Q2993585.title: Panjdeh incident
Q2993585.place: Panjdeh, on the Kushk and Murghab rivers (Afghan-Turkmen border)
paras: After taking Geok Tepe in 1881 and Merv (annexed in March 1884, according to Wikipedia; the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica's Merv article says the Russians occupied the oasis in 1883), Russia held most of what is now Turkmenistan, and its frontier with Afghanistan south of Merv was undefined. Britain, which saw the route from Merv through Herat and Kandahar as a road to India, agreed with Russia in 1884 to send a joint commission to mark the northern border of Afghanistan. Before it could start work, both sides pushed forward: Russian troops under General Komarov occupied posts to the south, while the Afghans garrisoned Panjdeh, an oasis of the Sarik Turkmens on the Murghab river, whose people said they were subjects of the Amir of Kabul.

In March 1885, at Panjdeh, the Russians attacked the Afghan troops and drove them out with heavy loss, taking their guns. Wikipedia dates the clash to 30 March (18 March in the Russian calendar) and quotes Komarov's report claiming that the Afghans had provoked him and lost more than 500 men. British officers on the spot had tried in vain to calm the situation.

The news caused a war scare in Britain. Wikipedia says that Gladstone asked parliament for a war credit of £11 million, partly for the Sudan, where Khartoum had fallen a few months earlier. The amir, Abdur Rahman, was at Rawalpindi meeting the viceroy of India, Lord Dufferin, when he heard of it; he chose to treat it as a border skirmish, which helped to calm the crisis.

The affair was settled diplomatically, as both the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia say: Russia kept Panjdeh and gave up Zulfikar, and the commission went on to mark the frontier up to the Oxus. Wikipedia dates the final protocol to 1887. The incident largely ended Russia's southward advance in Central Asia, apart from the Pamirs, and fixed Afghanistan's north-western border.

cp11-07.title: Congo Free State established
paras: In 1876 King Leopold II of the Belgians called a conference of geographers in Brussels, which created the International Association for the Exploration and Civilization of Africa. After Henry Morton Stanley's journey down the Congo, Leopold turned to that river: in 1878 a Committee for the Study of the Upper Congo was formed in Brussels, which became the International Association of the Congo. Working for it, and largely paid from the king's own purse, Stanley spent four years founding stations along the river and signing treaties with local chiefs.

Leopold then won the powers' recognition. The United States recognized the association as a state in April 1884 and Germany followed in November. At the Berlin Conference of 1884-85, according to Wikipedia, he persuaded the other European states that his work was humanitarian and that he would not tax trade. Treaties with France and Portugal in February 1885 fixed the borders on the lower Congo, with the north bank of the lower river going to the association and the south bank, as far as Noki, to Portugal.

In April 1885 the Belgian parliament allowed Leopold to become head of the new state, on condition that the union between Belgium and the Congo would be 'exclusively personal'. The state took the name Independent State of the Congo, known in English as the Congo Free State, and on 1 August 1885 Leopold informed the powers of its neutrality and its claimed borders. It belonged to the king himself, not to Belgium.

A decree of 1 July 1885 declared all 'vacant lands' the property of the state, and this was later read so as to leave the inhabitants only the land they lived on or farmed. Leopold's administration and the concession companies extracted ivory and rubber through forced labour, torture and killings; Wikipedia says the highest estimates put the deaths at half the population of the rubber districts. After an international outcry, the Belgian parliament annexed the Congo as a Belgian colony in 1908.

Q2604396.title: Witwatersrand Gold Rush
paras: Gold had been found in the Transvaal (the South African Republic) before, in small amounts on the Witwatersrand in the 1850s, according to Wikipedia, and in the eastern goldfields of Barberton and Pilgrim's Rest, which attracted attention from 1884. In 1886 the main gold reef of the Witwatersrand was found. Wikipedia credits the discovery of the main reef to George Harrison on the farm Langlaagte in July 1886, while noting that the prospector Jan Bantjes had found a reef in 1884; after Harrison registered his claim the government declared the area open to diggers.

Prospectors and fortune-seekers poured in from abroad. A mining camp grew on the reef, and in September 1886 the town of Johannesburg was founded. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says it was named after Johannes Rissik, the Transvaal surveyor-general; Wikipedia notes that the origin of the name is disputed. In December 1886 the Boer government marked out the town, and plots were handed to their buyers on 1 January 1887.

The main reef could be traced, the Britannica says, for about 62 miles, but the gold lay in tiny particles, in many places deep underground. After a slump in 1890, when the surface ore ran out, better machinery and cheaper coal brought a revival. According to the Britannica the yield rose from 23,000 ounces in 1887 to 1,210,000 in 1892 and 4,295,000 in 1898, and the republic's revenue, about £150,000 before the discovery, passed two million pounds in 1894. Railways linked the Rand to the coast in 1892-1895, and Johannesburg became the largest town in South Africa within ten years.

Most of the newcomers were foreigners, called Uitlanders, and their grievances against the Boer government of President Paul Kruger grew. They were followed by the failed Jameson Raid and Uitlander rising of 1895-96 and, a few years later, by the South African War of 1899-1902.

Q705537.title: Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty
paras: In the 'Scramble for Africa' Britain and Germany were rivals in East Africa, where the Sultanate of Zanzibar, once ruling a long stretch of the mainland coast, had seen its lands divided by Britain, Germany and Italy. The German East Africa Company of Carl Peters held a strip of the Tanganyika coast, but Germany had no control over the sultan's islands. Germany's new chancellor, Leo von Caprivi, wanted a settlement with Britain.

The agreement, signed on 1 July 1890, settled several disputes at once. Germany gained Heligoland, a small island group in the North Sea that Britain had seized from Denmark in 1807 and kept since 1814; the strip of land later called the Caprivi Strip, which gave German South-West Africa access to the Zambezi; and a free hand on the coast opposite Zanzibar that became the heart of German East Africa. In return Germany gave up its protectorate over Witu on the Kenyan coast and lands the British needed for a railway to Lake Victoria, and accepted British authority over Zanzibar. The treaty also fixed borders in West Africa, between Togoland and the Gold Coast and between Kamerun and Nigeria.

For Germany Heligoland mattered because it commanded the approaches to its North Sea ports and to the Kiel Canal, then being built. On 4 November 1890 Britain proclaimed a protectorate over Zanzibar, which was reduced to the islands of Zanzibar and Pemba, nominal rights over a ten-mile coastal strip and a few ports. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica adds that in a parallel arrangement Britain gave up its claims to Madagascar in favour of France.

Heligoland was joined to Prussia in 1892, and its people were given special rights. In Germany the treaty was attacked: Wikipedia says the misleading name 'Heligoland-Zanzibar' was coined by the former chancellor Otto von Bismarck to attack his successor, suggesting that Germany had swapped an African empire for a tiny island, and the outcry helped lead to the founding of the Pan-German League in 1891.

Q857982.title: First Matabele War
Q857982.place: Matabeleland (western Zimbabwe), from Fort Victoria to Bulawayo
paras: Under a royal charter, Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company sent a pioneer column in 1890 into Mashonaland, where it founded Fort Salisbury (now Harare). The Shona there had long been raided by the Ndebele (Matabele) kingdom of Lobengula, whose capital was Bulawayo. In July 1893 a large Ndebele force, sent to punish a Shona chief, raided Shona villages around the company's new town of Fort Victoria and entered its streets. The administrator of Mashonaland, Leander Starr Jameson, decided that only force would settle the matter.

Jameson's force was small: the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives about 700 volunteers and 225 Bechuanaland police with some 700 African allies. Columns from Fort Salisbury and Fort Victoria joined in October and marched on Bulawayo, while Khama's Bechuana (Tswana) men advanced from the south. The Ndebele regiments attacked the columns twice, near the Shangani river and on 1 November at Bembesi, but were cut down by rifles and machine guns (Maxims). The sources give different numbers: the Britannica says 4,000 to 5,000 Ndebele attacked at the Shangani and some 7,000 at the second fight; Wikipedia gives 3,500 at the Shangani with about 1,500 killed, against four company dead, and 2,000 riflemen and 4,000 warriors at Bembesi, of whom about 2,500 were killed.

Lobengula fled north and his capital was burned. On 3 November the columns entered Bulawayo. A column under Major Patrick Forbes pursued the king, and on 3-4 December Major Allan Wilson's advance party of 34 men crossed the Shangani river; the river rose behind them, and the Ndebele surrounded and killed them all, apart from three men sent back for help.

Lobengula died in January 1894, of fever or of a wound according to the Britannica, of smallpox according to Wikipedia. Matabeleland passed under the company's rule and, with Mashonaland, became the territory known as Rhodesia. The company's seizure of Ndebele cattle after the war was one of the grievances behind the later Ndebele rising.

Q916340.title: Jameson Raid
Q916340.place: From Mafeking, on the Bechuanaland border, to Doornkop, near Johannesburg
paras: After the gold discoveries of 1886 thousands of foreigners, the Uitlanders, came to the Transvaal (the South African Republic). They complained of their treatment by President Paul Kruger's Boer government. Cecil Rhodes, prime minister of Cape Colony and head of the British South Africa Company, backed a plan by Uitlander leaders in Johannesburg to rise in revolt, while a mounted force under Leander Starr Jameson, a colonial administrator in Rhodes's employ, waited on the border to ride in to their support.

The plot faltered. The Johannesburg leaders lacked arms, and they were divided, among other things over a hint from Cape Town that Rhodes wanted the revolt made under the British flag; at a meeting on 25 December, the Britannica says, they decided to postpone it. Jameson nevertheless crossed into the Transvaal on 29 December 1895 with about 600 men according to Wikipedia and the Britannica's Jameson article, most of them from the Matabeleland Mounted Police (the Britannica's article on Rhodes says some 500), and cut the telegraph wires so he could not be recalled. In Johannesburg a reform committee hurriedly took charge, but no rising took place.

Boer forces shadowed the column and stopped it at Doornkop, near Johannesburg, where Jameson surrendered on the promise that his men's lives would be spared; Wikipedia dates the surrender to 2 January 1896 (the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica's Transvaal article says the end of January, but its Jameson article puts the surrender before Johannesburg laid down its arms on 7 January). Kruger handed the raiders to the British government, and in London Jameson was sentenced to fifteen months in prison. The reform leaders were tried in Pretoria; four were condemned to death, the sentences later commuted, according to the Britannica, to fines of £25,000 each.

The raid had wide consequences. The German emperor William II sent Kruger a telegram congratulating him on repelling the raiders without the help of friendly powers, which angered Britain. Rhodes had to resign as prime minister of the Cape. With much of its police away, Rhodesia was left exposed, and the Ndebele rose in March 1896. Relations between Britain and the Transvaal grew worse, and Wikipedia counts the raid among the causes of the South African (Second Boer) War of 1899-1902.
